g.text: The Amazon is one of the longest rivers
in the world. Depending on how you
measure it, it runs somewhere between
6,400 and 7,000 kilometres, from the
Andes mountains in Peru all the way
east to the Atlantic coast of Brazil.
It carries more water than the next
seven largest rivers in the world
put together, about a fifth of all
the fresh water that flows into the
oceans. And yet, along that entire
length, there is not a single bridge
that crosses it. Why not just build
one? My first thought was that it
must simply be too wide. For most
of its length, the river is a few
kilometres across, widening to 10
kilometres or more near its lower
reaches. That is wide, but humans
have built far longer bridges. India's
Bogibeel Bridge over the Brahmaputra,
a river famous for flooding and shifting
its course, is almost 5 kilometres
long and carries both trains and cars.
The Congo, another enormous, wild
river, has had the Matadi Bridge across
it since 1983. Even India floods badly
every single year,
and we still build bridges over our
rivers. So width is not the problem.
Walter Kaufmann, a structural engineer
at ETH Zurich, points to two problems.
Few places along the river need a
bridge. For most of its length, the
Amazon runs through dense rainforest
with very few people and very few
roads. A bridge is only useful if
there is a road on both ends, and
along most of the Amazon there simply
is not. Where people do need to cross,
they use boats and ferries, which
have been moving people and goods
up and down the river for centuries.
Flooding makes bridge foundations
difficult to build. Every year, the
river rises by more than 9 metres
in the rainy season and spills into
the forest around it. In the wet season,
the flooded area grows from about
110,000 square kilometres to about
350,000, roughly the size of Germany.
The banks are soft, muddy and constantly
being reshaped by the water. A bridge
needs solid ground
to stand on, and the Amazon keeps
moving the ground. There is even a
second, hidden "river" under the ground.
In 2011, a team led by Valiya Hamza,
an Indian-born geophysicist at Brazil's
National Observatory, announced that
they had found another "river" flowing
under the Amazon, about 4 kilometres
underground. They worked it out from
temperature measurements in 241 old
oil wells, which suggested water was
slowly moving through the rock deep
below the surface. It runs about 6,000
kilometres, roughly following the
Amazon from west to east, and is 200
to 400 kilometres wide. It is not
a river in the way we usually picture
one, though. It is water seeping through
porous rock, moving at less than a
millimetre per second, slower than
most glaciers. The Amazon above it
moves at around 2 metres per second.
Hamza himself said he used the word
river "not in the conventional sense",
and many scientists think it should
not be called a river at all. So does
a second river underneath make the
ground even shakier for a bridge?
Probably not. At 4 kilometres deep,
it is far below where any bridge foundation
would reach. The ground problems engineers
worry about are the ones at the surface,
the floods, the mud and the moving
banks. A city of two million, cut
off A crossing
might make more sense at Manaus, the
biggest concentration of people anywhere
along the Amazon. It began in 1669
as a Portuguese fort at a river junction,
became one of the richest cities in
South America during the rubber boom
of the late 1800s, and then boomed
again after 1967, when Brazil turned
it into a tax-free industrial zone
and factories moved in. Today it is
home to about 2.3 million people,
all in one place surrounded by forest.
If a bridge makes sense anywhere,
it is here. There is still no paved
road connecting Manaus to the rest
of Brazil. One highway runs north
to Venezuela, and the one heading
south towards Porto Velho starts with
a ferry across the river and turns
into an unusable dirt track after
about 100 kilometres. Almost everything
and everyone arrives by boat or by
plane. Manaus does have one big bridge,
and that comes
down to where the city was built in
the first place. The old fort was
not placed on the main Amazon but
on the bank of the Rio Negro, its
biggest tributary, just before the
two rivers meet. So in 2011, when
Brazil finally built the Rio Negro
Bridge, a 3.6 kilometre cable-stayed
bridge to the town of Iranduba, it
crossed the Rio Negro, not the Amazon
itself. To reach the highway on the
south side of the main river, you
still need a ferry. The Rio Negro
is dark, almost black, because it
carries dissolved material from decaying
plants in the forest. The upper Amazon,
which Brazilians call the Solimões,
is pale and sandy, full of sediment
from the Andes. They flow side by
side for kilometres without mixing,
because they differ in temperature,
speed and density, so you can see
a sharp line down the middle of the
water. Locals call it the Meeting
of Waters. I
missed more meetings than I would
like to admit last week. Europe turned
its clocks back on October 25, but
the US only did it on November 1,
so for one whole week every transatlantic
meeting was an hour off from where
my brain thought it was. While I was
busy apologising to I started wondering
which countries even
bother with daylight saving time,
and I found out something strange.
Egypt is the only country in Africa
that does it. Why would Egypt need
to save daylight? At first this sounds
completely unnecessary. Daylight saving
time exists because places far from
the equator have very long summer
days and very short winter ones, so
shifting the clock moves some of that
extra summer light into the evening.
Egypt has plenty of light all year
round. And why would it be the only
one in all of Africa? The geography
backs up my confusion. Look at how
much the length of the day changes
over a year in three cities. London
gets less than 8 hours of daylight
in December and more than 16 in June,
so moving an hour of light around
actually makes a difference there.
Cairo only swings between about 10
and 14 hours, and near the equator
in Nairobi, the day is basically 12
hours long all year. Most of Africa
sits close to
the equator, which is why almost nobody
there bothers. The countries outside
Europe and North America that still
change their clocks, like Chile, New
Zealand, southern Australia and Israel,
all sit further from the equator,
and Egypt sits right at the edge of
where it starts to make sense. There
is always a colonial connection The
British first introduced summer time
in Egypt in 1940, during the Second
World War, when Egypt was a key British
military base. It stopped after the
war, came back in 1957, and then Egypt
spent the next several decades switching
it on and off. After the 2011 revolution,
the transitional government abolished
it. It came back in 2014, was cancelled
again in 2015 after the electricity
ministry said the savings were not
of "any tangible effect", and in 2016
the government famously cancelled
it just three days before the clocks
were supposed to change. Then, in
2023, it came back again. Energy Saving
Time When the
government restored it in 2023, the
stated reason was to save energy at
a time when fuel had become expensive
after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The less natural gas Egypt burns in
its own power plants, the more it
can sell to
Europe for much-needed foreign currency.
Egypt had exported around $600 million
of gas to Europe the year before and
was hoping to reach $1 billion, and
the electricity ministry estimated
the clock change would save about
$25 million worth of gas. This doesn't
completely make sense to me though,
because the heat is the same no matter
what the clock says. In a hot country,
the biggest demand on the power grid
is not lights, it's air conditioning.
Shifting the clock means people are
home and awake during the hottest
part of the evening, possibly running
their air conditioners even more.
And there is research suggesting exactly
that. When parts of Indiana adopted
daylight saving time, economists used
it as a natural experiment and found
that it actually increased household
electricity use by about 1%, mostly
because the savings on lighting were
wiped out by extra heating and cooling.
Egypt's own electricity ministry reached
a similar conclusion
back in 2015, which might explain
why the country keeps switching it
on and off. Morocco’s clocks? Morocco,
the other North African country with
complicated clocks, used to permanently
run an hour ahead and briefly switch
back during Ramadan, but it returned
to plain GMT this September, leaving
Egypt truly alone. As for me, I have
now put every time zone into my calendar,
so hopefully next spring goes better
than this autumn did. Today I came
across the word bomba, Polish for
"bomb", and learnt that it was the
name of a machine built in 1938 by
a Polish mathematician called Marian
Rejewski to break the German Enigma
cipher. My first reaction was confusion.
If the Poles had a machine to break
Enigma in 1938, then what was Alan
Turing doing? I grew up thinking Turing
broke Enigma, full stop. Enigma was
never just one machine Enigma looked
like a typewriter in a wooden box.
Every time you pressed a key, an electrical
signal passed through
a set of rotating wheels called rotors
and a panel of plug cables, and a
different letter lit up. Then the
rotors turned, so pressing the same
key again gave a completely different
letter. With all the possible rotor
orders, starting positions and plug
connections, the number of ways to
set up the machine ran into the trillions
and beyond, and the Germans changed
the settings every day. What I did
not realise is that Enigma was not
one fixed machine that someone broke
once. The Germans kept changing the
hardware and the rules for using it,
and every change meant the codebreakers
had to break it again. Version one,
broken by a repeated word Poland had
